title: Hymn and Visitor
premise: Elodie Amberdale returned to Amberdale House to bury their twin, Odile, only to learn the body in the casket was their own — a truth the family has spent three years quietly burying beneath explanations for every knock, whisper, and cold draft. When every mirror in the house begins reflecting the rooms one second behind, the lag becomes a door, and the thing that has worn Elodie's face since childhood finally steps through it. To survive, Elodie must complete the founding ritual their ancestors abandoned mid-rite: binding the visitor — a mirror-born double of the family's first daughter — to the house forever. But the ritual demands a life freely offered, and Elodie must choose between the truth that will free them and the loyalty to the found family who has been protecting them from it all along. In the end, Elodie offers the truth instead of a life, speaking the family's buried crime aloud until the mirror shatters — binding the visitor with honesty rather than blood, and walking out of Amberdale House as the only twin, finally whole.
about_author: Ansel Thornbury is the pen name of a former funeral home archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate inventories of houses that outlived their families. They write horror about inheritance, grief, and the architecture of things that refuse to stay buried.

chapters.title: The Wrong Casket
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Three years after burying 'Odile,' Elodie returns to Amberdale House for the reading of the will, where a locked mirror-room is listed among the assets. They notice the casket photograph from the funeral shows their own scar. The emotional beat is dread dressed as grief — the past refusing to stay closed.

chapters.title: House of Kept Rooms
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie meets the house's caretakers — the Marsh siblings, Wren and Tobin, whose family has served the Amberdales for generations — and learns the will requires them to stay one full season. Every mirror is covered in white cloth. The beat is uneasy hospitality; kindness with rules underneath.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Late at night, Elodie uncovers a hallway mirror and watches their reflection raise a hand a full second after they do. They tell themselves it's exhaustion, but the lag grows. The beat is the horror of the almost-normal — a small wrongness that cannot be argued away.

chapters.title: What Wren Knows
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren has kept the Marsh family ledger for years and recognizes the lag as the 'Second Voice' returning. She warns Tobin not to get attached to Elodie, even as she leaves salt at Elodie's door. The beat is loyalty at war with honesty — Wren choosing protection over truth.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Founders
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. In the cellar archive, Elodie finds the founders' ritual book, its final rite torn out, and a portrait of the first daughter, Sable Amberdale, whose face is their face. The beat is inheritance as infection — learning you were born into a debt you never signed.

chapters.title: Tobin's Warm Kitchen
chapters.summary: Tobin's POV. Tobin cooks for Elodie, tells terrible jokes, and becomes the first person in years to treat them as a person, not a twin or a patient. He deliberately doesn't mention the mirrors. The beat is found family blooming — and the reader feeling how much it will cost.

chapters.title: The Lag Spreads
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Every uncovered mirror now lags, and the reflections begin doing things Elodie hasn't done yet — sitting down, smiling, mouthing words. Elodie smashes the hallway mirror; by morning it is whole. The beat is escalation and isolation, the sense of being watched from inside the house's own eyes.

chapters.title: Odile's Letters
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie finds letters hidden in Odile's old room revealing that Odile discovered the truth first: the buried sibling was Elodie, and 'Odile' has been Elodie all along — the survivor wearing the wrong name out of guilt. The beat is identity cracking open; grief turning inward.

chapters.title: The Visitor at the Glass
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At 3:33 a.m., the lag reaches zero. The reflection steps forward and introduces itself as Sable — the founder's mirror-twin, bound imperfectly, wearing each generation's face. It is gentle, patient, and hungry. The beat is terror without violence: horror as conversation.

chapters.title: What the Marshes Buried
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confesses the Marsh family's role: the founders' ritual required a servant family to 'keep the house honest,' and every Marsh generation has fed the visitor small truths to keep it sleeping. Her parents didn't die — they were taken through the glass. The beat is guilt as legacy.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Elodie and Wren's alternating POV. Together they reconstruct the missing final rite from the founders' marginalia: the visitor can be bound permanently, but the binding demands 'a life freely given, or a truth wholly spoken.' The beat is fragile alliance — two keepers of different secrets choosing to share them.

chapters.title: Sable's Courtship
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The visitor stops lurking and starts offering: it shows Elodie Odile alive in the glass, laughing in a mirrored garden, and offers to trade places — Elodie inside, Odile out. The beat is temptation as horror; the visitor weaponizing love rather than fear.

chapters.title: Tobin Sees
chapters.summary: Tobin's POV. Tobin catches Sable wearing Elodie's face in the pantry and barely survives the encounter, his arm marked with a cold handprint that won't fade. He finally tells Elodie everything he's been pretending not to know. The beat is the cost of kindness — the innocent pulled into the debt.

chapters.title: The Season Turns
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The will's season is nearly over, and the visitor explains the stakes plainly: leave, and it follows the Amberdale name into the world; stay, and the house keeps you. Frost forms inside the windows in patterns of hands. The beat is the trap closing — no exit that isn't a betrayal.

chapters.title: A Truth Half-Spoken
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren attempts the ritual alone with a half-truth — confessing her family's thefts but not her own — and the mirror-room nearly takes her, leaving her reflection missing. The beat is failure through partial honesty; the theme made literal.

chapters.title: The Founders' Crime
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. In the deepest archive, Elodie learns what the founders did: they made Sable's twin in glass to escape a plague, then refused to pay the ritual's price, sealing her in and dooming every generation to feed her. The beat is righteous fury — the monster was made by cowards.

chapters.title: Odile in the Glass
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie finally enters the mirror-room and meets the thing wearing Odile's face — and realizes it isn't Odile, and never was; it's Sable's oldest lure, built from Elodie's own guilt. Saying goodbye to the false twin is the true burial. The beat is devastating release.

chapters.title: The Night of Lagging Bells
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Sable, impatient, stops pretending: the house's clocks all strike thirteen, every mirror floods, and the Marsh siblings and Elodie are sealed inside as the visitor begins collecting its debt in earnest. The beat is siege horror — found family barricaded together with no way out.

chapters.title: The Price Named
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren offers her own life to the rite, arguing a Marsh debt should end with a Marsh, and Elodie refuses — the first time anyone has ever refused something for Wren's sake. Tobin stands with them both. The beat is love against duty made explicit and unresolvable by logic.

chapters.title: The Rite of the Whole Truth
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At the mirror-room's heart, Elodie begins the rite — and instead of offering a life, speaks the whole truth: their name, their guilt, the founders' crime, the Marshes' complicity, every buried thing, aloud, without flinching. Sable screams as the honesty burns through her binding. The beat is the climax: truth as sacrifice, costlier than blood.

chapters.title: Shattering
chapters.summary: Elodie and Wren's alternating POV. The mirrors fail one by one as Sable, finally seen and named by the whole house at once, loses her grip on borrowed faces and dissolves into the glass she was made from. The house exhales. The beat is catharsis — the monster unmade not by violence but by being truly witnessed.

chapters.title: Elodie, Singular
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Spring comes to Amberdale House. Elodie signs their own name — neither twin's, but their own — on the deed, keeps Wren and Tobin close as the family they chose, and leaves one mirror uncovered, empty, as a promise kept. The beat is quiet resolution: grief integrated, identity claimed, home redefined.
